clue.text: 1,000 in two lots of cash? I thought his assets were frozen!

definitions.text: I thought his assets were frozen!
definitions.note: an exclamation standing for the thing it alludes to, a noun

parts.note: brass is British slang for money, the first lot

indicators.note: a thing placed in another sits inside it, splitting the outer word around it

parts.note: the plain word for cash, the second lot
K = a thousand, as in a salary of 50K

explanation.surface: Someone is startled to learn a wealthy man's funds have been frozen by the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the British saying that it is cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey; 'assets' is a cheeky stand-in for what freezes.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom about bitter cold claims such weather would freeze a certain metal figure's private parts, which the exclamation mocks.

clue.text: Dog runs past

parts.note: R = runs, the cricket scoring abbreviation
over = past, as in 'the storm is over'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dog racing by; 'past' looks like a preposition but supplies the second chunk as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional name given to pet hounds, so it serves as a generic word for a canine.

clue.text: Exhausted, catching eastern river snake

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, wrapping round it

parts.note: spent = exhausted, worn out
E = eastern, compass abbreviation
R = river, map abbreviation

explanation.surface: A tired traveller in the east manages to catch a river snake.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Exhausted' makes it look like a description of the catcher; it is the word that does the catching.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal or biblical word for the same legless reptile, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Maiden race meeting — might it bring luck?

parts.note: M = maiden, a cricket scoring abbreviation for an over with no runs
Ascot is the famous English racecourse and its royal race meeting

explanation.surface: A first-time runner at a race meeting, and someone wondering what might bring it luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden race' looks like a race for horses that have never won; split it, and 'maiden' is only a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm, animal or figure kept by a team because people believe it brings good fortune.

clue.text: Storyteller climbing Scottish island hill

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means going upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A storyteller climbing a hill on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Arran is a Scottish island in the Firth of Clyde, and a tor is a rocky hilltop of the kind found on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tells or recounts a tale, a plain synonym for the teller.

clue.text: Elevate nurse, 50, hampered by broken bone

parts.note: EN = enrolled nurse, a crossword regular

indicators.note: to be hampered is to be hemmed in, so one piece is held inside another
a broken thing is out of its proper shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters
L = 50 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A fifty-year-old nurse with a broken bone needs raising up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevate nurse' reads like a care instruction, but 'Elevate' is the definition and 'nurse' starts the wordplay; the 50 sits inside the broken bone.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise someone to the peerage or to lift them morally, both senses of raising in rank.

clue.text: Belfast barge foundering — daughter completely shocked

indicators.note: a foundering vessel is breaking up and sinking, so the letters fall apart and regroup

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
D = daughter, genealogy abbreviation

explanation.surface: A barge sinks at Belfast and a daughter watching is left utterly stunned.
explanation.walkthrough: The city and the boat supply all but one letter; D for daughter completes the thirteen.
explanation.definitionFit: Stunned with astonishment, a colourful word for being overwhelmed by surprise.

clue.text: Sailors in the drink

parts.note: AB = able seaman, so ABS are sailors
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailors overboard and floundering in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea, so the surface is sailors overboard; only the last word is the definition, and 'in the' is read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong green aniseed spirit, one particular kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Swimming for those who are unsuited?

definitions.text: Swimming for those who are unsuited?

parts.note: surface reading: people unfit or ill-matched for something
setter's reading: people with no swimsuit on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsuited' normally means unsuitable; here it means literally without a suit, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathing naked in open water, which is exactly what someone lacking a costume would do.

clue.text: Organ I have held by both hands

indicators.note: something held is gripped on either side, so it sits between the holders

parts.note: L = left hand and R = right hand
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: Someone holding an organ carefully in both hands, perhaps a surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both hands' gives two letters, left and right, which sit on either side like bookends.
explanation.definitionFit: The large abdominal gland that filters blood is one of the body's internal organs.

clue.text: International player fine after season with Bath, initially

parts.note: spring is one of the four seasons

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word before it is kept

parts.note: first letter of the city name
OK = fine, all right

explanation.surface: An international rugby player does well after a season playing for Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is an English rugby club, which makes the surface convincing; 'fine' comes first in the clue but last in the answer, placed 'after' the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the South African national rugby side, named after the antelope, plays international matches.

clue.text: Where Banco Real goes bust?

indicators.note: something that goes bust collapses, so its letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A Spanish bank collapses somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Real Madrid are Barcelona's great football rivals, so the whole clue also reads as the place where Real gets beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: The Catalan city is where rival club Real Madrid would like to win but often lose.

clue.text: Little 'un I found in farm building

indicators.note: a thing found in a place is inside it, enclosed by it

parts.note: a barn stores hay and grain
taken as written

explanation.surface: A small child discovered in a barn on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Scottish word, which may be unfamiliar outside Britain: it simply means a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish and northern English dialect for a child, a young one.

clue.text: Bankers at Zürich admitting fake

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the words before it hold the answer within their letters

parts.note: runs from the end of the first word through the second into the start of the city

explanation.surface: Swiss bankers own up to a forgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitting' suggests a confession by the bankers; here it means letting the answer in, spanning BankERS AT Zürich.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from German, the word describes an inferior imitation substituted for the genuine article.

clue.text: Morse novel located in a rural county

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

parts.note: set = located, as in 'a film set in Paris'

indicators.note: novel means new, so the name is made new by rearranging it

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: An Inspector Morse novel set in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse is Colin Dexter's Oxford detective, so 'Morse novel' reads as a book title; 'novel' is the anagram signal. Somerset is a largely rural county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An English shire known for cider and farmland, fitting the description of an agricultural region.

clue.text: City firm really concealing books

parts.note: CO = company

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: very = really, as in 'very good'
NT = New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A City firm hiding its accounts, a financial scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City firm' suggests the City of London's finance houses, and 'books' suggests accounts; 'City' is the definition, an English city in the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral city in the West Midlands of England, one example of an urban centre.

clue.text: Fight involving female supporter with big hair

definitions.note: the clue names the hairstyle as a noun; the answer is usually its adjective or noun

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a bout is a fight, as in boxing
F = female
a fan supports a team or star

explanation.surface: A scrap breaks out involving a woman fan with a towering hairdo.
explanation.walkthrough: F and FAN sit side by side inside the fight, so the answer has a double F in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairstyle backcombed and puffed up high and round, so voluminous styled locks.

clue.text: Plucky performance in light-entertainment programme?

parts.note: game = plucky, willing, as in 'game for anything'
a show is a performance

explanation.surface: A contestant puts in a brave effort on a television quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: Game in the sense of plucky (willing to have a go) is the less common meaning, hidden behind the programme sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A television format where contestants compete for prizes, a staple of lightweight broadcasting.

clue.text: Lower classification of Nautilus, maybe?

parts.note: surface reading: a category below another in a biological taxonomy, since the nautilus is a mollusc
setter's reading: Nautilus is Captain Nemo's submarine, so the clue asks what kind of vessel it is

explanation.walkthrough: The nautilus is a real shelled sea creature, which makes the zoological reading natural; Jules Verne's Nautilus was a submarine, so it is of the 'sub' type.
explanation.definitionFit: A subordinate category within a broader group, and split in two it describes the vessel's category.

clue.text: Notes Ms Moore has gold piercing

indicators.note: something piercing goes right into another thing and sits within it

parts.note: Demi Moore, the American actress
OR = gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: An actress shows off a gold piercing.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for gold comes from heraldry and is a crossword staple; Demi Moore is an American film actress.
explanation.definitionFit: The first three syllables of the sol-fa scale, each naming a musical pitch.

clue.text: One page in dictionary (American) is kind of complex

definitions.note: the name is used attributively, as in 'Oedipus complex'

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

parts.note: OED = Oxford English Dictionary, then US = American
I = one, the Roman numeral
P = page

explanation.surface: A dictionary page tells us about an American complex.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(American)' looks like a note on the dictionary's spelling, but it supplies the final two letters, and one page goes in between.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud named a child's desire for the opposite-sex parent after the Greek king, giving the psychological term.

clue.text: Food store, pub fitted in old Greek precinct

indicators.note: something fitted in is installed inside a larger thing

parts.note: a deli sells cooked meats and cheeses
PH = public house, as marked on British maps

explanation.surface: A delicatessen and a pub squeezed into an ancient Greek site.
explanation.walkthrough: PH for pub comes from British Ordnance Survey maps, where it marks a public house.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient sanctuary of Apollo, home of the oracle, is a sacred enclosure from antiquity.

clue.text: Quiet massage that could be in bed

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for a noun

parts.note: sh = a call for quiet
a rub is a massage

explanation.surface: A gentle, quiet massage that might happen in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a garden flower bed, not the bedroom the massage suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A woody bush that gardeners plant in borders among flowers.

clue.text: I flirted giddily with Penny, getting day out of school?

indicators.note: a giddy thing spins dizzily, so the letters whirl into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
P = penny, the coin abbreviation

explanation.surface: A pupil confesses to flirting with a girl called Penny while skipping school.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a girl's name; it is only a coin. 'Day out of school' reads as truancy but is a sanctioned excursion.
explanation.definitionFit: An educational excursion where pupils leave the classroom to study somewhere else.

clue.text: Briefly survey sports ground supported by church

indicators.note: in a down clue a supported thing sits on top, so the other piece goes underneath

parts.note: rec = recreation ground, a British public playing field
CE = Church of England

explanation.surface: A quick look round a playing field that sits beside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' is part of the definition: the answer is a shortened form of reconnaissance, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Military slang, clipped from reconnaissance, for inspecting an area before acting.

clue.text: Record including pieces backed by remix of YMCA for the other side

indicators.note: to include is to take inside, so the outer piece wraps the rest

parts.note: EP = extended-play record

indicators.note: backed means sent backwards, so the letters run the other way
a remix re-edits a track, so the letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: men = pieces in chess or draughts
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A record featuring a remix of the Village People's YMCA on its B-side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other side' hints at a record's flip side, but here it means the opposition.
explanation.definitionFit: The opposing force's base, standing for adversaries in general, as in going over to it.

clue.text: Nut seen entering Cape Canaveral

indicators.note: something seen going into a place is visible inside it, sitting within its letters

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A crank spotted going into the Florida space centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' looks like a person, an eccentric; it is the definition in its plain food sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The edible kernel of a North American hickory, one kind of tree fruit.

clue.text: Items strewn around part of the capital

indicators.note: things lying around are scattered in no order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: Litter scattered around a district of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strewn' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: both words are needed for eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The London borough containing Parliament and the Abbey is one district of Britain's chief city.
